items.prompt:
I dictated this on a walk. Before I clean it up, tell me whether the argument holds.

ok so the thing about evals is everyone builds the grader after they build the thing which means the grader just measures whatever the thing already does, and then you ship and it turns out the grader was measuring the wrong stuff the whole time, and i think the fix is you write the failing case first the same way you would with a test but nobody does that for prose
items.source_text: ok so the thing about evals is everyone builds the grader after they build the thing which means the grader just measures whatever the thing already does, and then you ship and it turns out the grader was measuring the wrong stuff the whole time, and i think the fix is you write the failing case first the same way you would with a test but nobody does that for prose
items.output:
I think the core argument holds up well: current evals are a feedback loop with themselves. The grader is a mirror of the builder's expectations, and a mirror only shows you what you already believe.

The two fatal flaws in the current method are:

1. **Selection bias:** The developer-grader grades its own output.
2. **Missing signal:** It measures the wrong assumptions.

The fix—writing failing cases before the implementation—is the right one, but it needs a concrete mechanism. For a coding agent, that might mean a task and a verifiable outcome. For prose, it might mean a held-out set of requirements and a blind grader.

items.prompt: Write a 600-word Field Note arguing that code review comments should expire after a week if nobody acts on them. Make the strongest version of the argument, then the strongest objection to it.
items.output:
I was looking at a stale pull request from last Tuesday. The thread had seven comments, three questions, and one task. I hadn't touched it since Friday, and the author hadn't replied. The real world moved on, but that PR still sat in the queue, claiming attention that was no longer relevant.

I still think the thread has a good point, but the context has changed. The API surface shifted, a dependency was bumped, and the original task is now part of a larger refactor. If you don't act on a comment within a week, it should expire. Not because the feedback is wrong, but because the context has moved.

Use the first week to debate the architecture, question the API surface, and test the edge cases. If the discussion stays stuck on one detail for days, the team hasn't solved the friction, and the comments become clutter. A working tree with stale comments is worse than a working tree with no comments at all.

The real world doesn't stop when a pull request does. A week in a fast-moving repo is a long time. The work starts somewhere else, and the developer moves on to the next big thing. If you leave a comment unaddressed for seven days, the team should assume the context has shifted and revisit it when the work actually returns to that state.

![A stale pull request sits in a queue with seven comments, three questions, and one task.](/img/writing/stalled-pr-queue.png)

items.prompt: Open a post with a quoted objection from a skeptical reader, then answer it. Topic: why I keep a local model instead of calling a hosted one.
items.output:
"I don't see the point in running a local model when you can call a hosted API and get a much larger base model for a fraction of the inference cost."

That's the trap: the hosted model is a better coder, and it's cheaper per token. But for a developer-first agent, that trade-off breaks down fast.

When you call a hosted API, you have zero control over the system prompt, the tool call harness, or the context window. With a local model, I can run the same 8B or 12B base across different harness versions and compare the exact pass rates. I can also inspect the raw logprobs and harness-level traces before making a decision.

The real reason is privacy and data residency. I don't want my team's proprietary repository being used to train a model at 2am. Running locally, the data never leaves our network, and our system prompt stays under our version control.

It doesn't replace GPT-4 or Claude 3 Opus for heavy architectural work. But for task-based agent skills like reading docs, writing boilerplate, and running terminal commands, a local model with a dedicated harness is the most efficient way to ship fast.

items.prompt: Draft two paragraphs on what I got wrong about developer onboarding metrics. Write it as something I am admitting, not something I am teaching.
items.output:
I used to think the only metric that mattered was "Time to First Hello World." I kept hitting it, then I'd hit the same blockers again two weeks later. I was measuring the wrong assumptions. The real bottleneck wasn't the first line of code; it was the five hours of configuration and the three missing API keys hidden in a thread from last year.

I also over-indexed on "active daily API calls." A developer can spam a surface area with useless requests and still be a top contributor. I had to stop counting surface area and start looking at the work that actually moved the needle. The highest-signal insights came from watching a developer hit real blockers on live data, not just in a sandbox.

items.output: I had to move across the country in late July, and my sourdough starter was sitting on the kitchen counter looking like a science project gone wrong. It had two days of neglect and a layer of gray liquid on top. I wasn't sure it would survive the move, let alone the move-in day.

items.prompt: Write about what telemetry from a sim racing lap taught you that watching the replay did not.
items.output:
I was looking at the telemetry from a late-braking move into Turn 1 at Spa. The replay looked good: I hit the apex perfectly, and the car stayed flat through the exit. But when I looked at the data, the truth was different.

I had over-braked by 400 meters, wasting tire life and opening up a gap for the car behind. I had also braked too late into the corner, sacrificing mid-corner speed to make up the time I lost at the end of the straight. The replay hid the fact that I was driving defensively instead of fast.

The telemetry showed the exact moment my brake pressure collapsed and when my tire temps spiked. That is the level of detail you need.

items.prompt: Write a short piece about learning to sail in your thirties and being bad at it in public.
items.output:
I was forty and it looked like I had a bad answer in my head: what was the point of learning to sail when I was already a senior manager and a father? I figured I had reached my peak and it was time to let the younger generation take the wheel.

But then I actually stepped on a boat in a heavy swell.

I had spent twenty years in boardrooms and committee meetings. I was used to controlling the room, directing the strategy, and being the expert in the room. Sailing stripped that away immediately. The ocean doesn't care about your job title or your LinkedIn endorsements. It doesn't care how much you paid for the boat either.

The first time I really struggled, I was at a dock in a heavy swell, trying to tie a cleat hitch while the boat was pitching around me. I was sweating, swearing under my breath, and fumbling with the rope like a teenager. A group of sailors at the next dock watched me struggle. I could feel their eyes on me, judging my technique and my lack of sea-sense.

I felt that old one i had in my head: "What if they see me fail?"

The real world doesn't work that way, though. Most people are too busy with their own lives to judge your mistakes. The sailors at the next dock weren't looking down on me; they were watching to see if I could hold up against the wind.

I kept coming back. I kept hitting the pier at twoam and getting salt in my eyes. I kept getting the lines tangled. But each time, the muscle memory got better. The panic moved from my throat to my gut, where it was easier to manage.

If you don't test yourself against something that can actually hurt you, you have no idea where your real edges are.

items.prompt: Write about restoring a film camera whose light meter lies by two stops.
items.output:
I was at a computer monitor with a senior engineer and I asked him about the most important thing he learned in his first year. He looked me straight in the eye and said, "Trust, but verify. If you don't test your assumptions against a baseline, you have no idea where you actually are."

That baseline is the one thing my old Nikon FE's light meter had lost. It was guessing, and it was guessing big—by as much as two stops in certain light. In a world of digital precision, that kind of drift is a fatal defect.

The repair was straightforward: a clean and re-lubricated shutter, a new light meter cell, and a recalibrated circuit. But the real work was in the restore: making sure the camera behaved exactly like it did when it was new, even after years of neglect.

I wrote the repair notes in my field journal, detailing every resistance change and timing offset. The most important lesson was simple: a reliable tool doesn't need to be the fastest in the room, but it has to be the most honest.

items.prompt: Write about coaching a youth soccer team where nobody wants to play defense.
items.output:
I was at the field with a group of ten-year-olds and I had a problem: every single kid wanted to be the striker. When you asked a kid to play defense, they looked at you like you were asking them to do their taxes.

I had to go back to basics: what did they actually want, and what did the team need? I cut the field size in half and put custom colored cones on the field. If you were in the blue zone, you couldn't touch the ball. If you were in the red zone, you could. That gave them boundaries without me having to yell "get back on defense."

The real lesson was simple: give them choice, but give it within a boundary. If you don't ship the smallest useful version of your product, you never get the feedback you need to grow.

items.prompt: Write about opening a home electrical panel, deciding not to touch it, and calling somebody.
items.output: I opened the door to my breaker panel and looked at the wiring. It looked like a bird had nested inside a box of tangled copper. I had a good answer for each wire, but then I stopped. I had two choices: I could force it, or I could call an electrician and pay the highest hourly rate they had.
